Below is a comprehensive tutorial blog post based on your project titled Dynamic Network Analysis and Graph-Based Insights with Pandas, complete with explanations, code breakdowns, and references. You can copy‑and‑paste the full code at the end to run it immediately.

Summary

In Dynamic Network Analysis and Graph-Based Insights with Pandas, we’ll use the Titanic passenger data to construct and explore dynamic graphs. You’ll learn to load tabular data into a graph, compute key network metrics (like degree centrality), find shortest paths, detect communities with modularity maximization, and visualize your results using Pandas, NetworkX, and Matplotlib. This tutorial covers:

  • Project Goals: Transform tabular data into networks and extract insights.
  • Lessons Learned: How graph theory concepts apply to real data.
  • Core Concepts: Graph construction, centrality, shortest‐path algorithms, community detection (Clauset–Newman–Moore), and force‐directed layouts.
  • Dataset Explained: Titanic passenger manifest with cabins, names, etc.
  • Inputs: Passenger names, cabin assignments, and optional source/target passenger pairs.

Project Description

This project pushes your understanding of Pandas by incorporating network analysis techniques to analyze and visualize relationships in datasets. Using Pandas in combination with NetworkX and Matplotlib, you will:

  1. Construct networks from structured data (e.g., link passengers sharing the same cabin).
  2. Compute centrality measures (degree centrality to identify “important” passengers).
  3. Find shortest paths between any two passengers in the network.
  4. Detect communities using greedy modularity maximization.
  5. Visualize the resulting graph with node sizes proportional to centrality.

Lesson to Be Learned

By the end of this tutorial, you’ll be able to:

  • Map tabular data to graph structures using NetworkX.
  • Compute network metrics like degree centrality to identify influential nodes (passengers).
  • Trace connections via shortest‑path algorithms to explore indirect relationships.
  • Uncover communities within your data using greedy modularity maximization.
  • Produce insightful visualizations that reveal hidden patterns in your network.

Concepts Used

  • Pandas DataFrame: Flexible tabular data structure for loading and manipulating CSV data (Pandas).
  • NetworkX Graphs: Python library for creating and analyzing graphs and networks (Wikipedia).
  • Degree Centrality: Fraction of nodes directly connected to a given node (NetworkX).
  • Shortest Path: Dijkstra and other path‑finding algorithms highlight connectivity (Wikipedia).
  • Greedy Modularity Communities: Clauset–Newman–Moore method to detect clusters (NetworkX).
  • Spring Layout: Force‑directed layout for graph visualization (Wikipedia).
  • Matplotlib Pyplot: MATLAB‑like plotting interface for Python (Matplotlib).
  • Tabular‑to‑Graph Mapping: Grouping and linking rows based on shared attributes.

Dataset and Inputs

We use the Titanic dataset (CSV with columns like Name, Cabin, Ticket, etc.). Key fields:

  • Name: Passenger identifier (used as graph nodes).
  • Cabin: Cabin code (used to link passengers sharing the same cabin).

Optional inputs include:

  • source and target names for shortest‑path exploration.
  • family name grouping for alternate centrality computations.

Code Walkthrough

1. Loading Data & Libraries

import pandas as pd
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load Titanic Dataset
file_path = "titanic.xlsx"
df = pd.read_excel(file_path)

We read the CSV into a Pandas DataFrame, the primary data container for analysis (Pandas).

2. Create Passenger Network Based on Shared Cabin

def create_cabin_network(df):
    G = nx.Graph()
    for _, group in df.groupby("Cabin"):
        names = group["Name"].tolist()
        for i in range(len(names)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(names)):
                G.add_edge(names[i], names[j])
    return G
  • Group by Cabin to find all passengers sharing that cabin.
  • Add edges between every pair in the group, building an undirected graph.

3. Calculate Centrality Metrics

def calculate_centrality_metrics(graph):
    centrality = nx.degree_centrality(graph)
    return (
        pd.DataFrame(centrality.items(), columns=["Passenger", "Centrality"])
          .sort_values(by="Centrality", ascending=False)
    )
  • Degree centrality measures how many direct connections each node has, normalized by n−1 (NetworkX).

4. Shortest Path Analysis

def shortest_path_between(graph, source, target):
    if nx.has_path(graph, source, target):
        return nx.shortest_path(graph, source=source, target=target)
    else:
        return f"No path exists between {source} and {target}."
  • Uses Dijkstra’s algorithm (or BFS for unweighted graphs) to find the shortest connection (Wikipedia).

5. Visualize Network with Metrics

def visualize_network(graph, centrality=None, title="Passenger Network"):
    pos = nx.spring_layout(graph)  # Force‑directed layout :contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 12))
    if centrality:
        sizes = [v * 1000 for v in centrality.values()]
        nx.draw_networkx_nodes(graph, pos, node_size=sizes)
    else:
        nx.draw_networkx_nodes(graph, pos, node_size=300)
    nx.draw_networkx_edges(graph, pos, alpha=0.3)
    nx.draw_networkx_labels(graph, pos, font_size=10)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.show()
  • Spring layout positions nodes to reveal clusters and relationships.
  • Node sizes reflect centrality when provided.

6. Community Detection

def detect_communities(graph):
    communities = nx.algorithms.community.greedy_modularity_communities(graph)
    return [list(c) for c in communities]
  • Greedy modularity maximization groups nodes to maximize intra‑community density (NetworkX).

Complete Code Listing

import pandas as pd
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load Titanic Dataset
file_path = "titanic.xlsx"
df = pd.read_excel(file_path)

# 1. Create Passenger Network Based on Shared Cabin
def create_cabin_network(df):
    G = nx.Graph()
    for _, group in df.groupby("Cabin"):
        names = group["Name"].tolist()
        for i in range(len(names)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(names)):
                G.add_edge(names[i], names[j])
    return G

# 2. Calculate Centrality Metrics
def calculate_centrality_metrics(graph):
    centrality = nx.degree_centrality(graph)
    return (
        pd.DataFrame(centrality.items(), columns=["Passenger", "Centrality"])
          .sort_values(by="Centrality", ascending=False)
    )

# 3. Shortest Path Analysis
def shortest_path_between(graph, source, target):
    if nx.has_path(graph, source, target):
        return nx.shortest_path(graph, source=source, target=target)
    else:
        return f"No path exists between {source} and {target}."

# 4. Visualize Network with Metrics
def visualize_network(graph, centrality=None, title="Passenger Network"):
    pos = nx.spring_layout(graph)
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 12))
    if centrality:
        sizes = [v * 1000 for v in centrality.values()]
        nx.draw_networkx_nodes(graph, pos, node_size=sizes)
    else:
        nx.draw_networkx_nodes(graph, pos, node_size=300)
    nx.draw_networkx_edges(graph, pos, alpha=0.3)
    nx.draw_networkx_labels(graph, pos, font_size=10)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.show()

# 5. Community Detection
def detect_communities(graph):
    communities = nx.algorithms.community.greedy_modularity_communities(graph)
    return [list(c) for c in communities]

# Test the pipeline
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("1) Building cabin-based network…")
    cabin_network = create_cabin_network(df)
    print(f"Nodes: {len(cabin_network.nodes)}; Edges: {len(cabin_network.edges)}")
    
    print("\n2) Computing centrality…")
    centrality_df = calculate_centrality_metrics(cabin_network)
    print(centrality_df.head())
    
    print("\n3) Shortest path between top two central nodes…")
    s, t = centrality_df.iloc[0, 0], centrality_df.iloc[1, 0]
    print(shortest_path_between(cabin_network, s, t))
    
    print("\n4) Visualizing network…")
    visualize_network(cabin_network, centrality=nx.degree_centrality(cabin_network))
    
    print("\n5) Detecting communities…")
    comms = detect_communities(cabin_network)
    print(f"Detected {len(comms)} communities; e.g., {comms[0]}")

Further Extensions

  • Alternate Relations: Build graphs linking passengers by ticket number or family name.
  • Other Centralities: Compute betweenness or eigenvector centrality for deeper insights (NetworkX).
  • Interactive Visuals: Use Plotly or Bokeh for web‑based interactive network plots.
  • Large‑Scale Graphs: Explore more efficient community algorithms (e.g., Louvain) for bigger datasets (NetworkX).
